Noah (Arca noae) exhibits a maximum shell length of approximately 7 centimeters, with the ultimate shell height reaching 3.5 cm [Li = 3.5 cm] in large, presumably senescent individuals collected from the eastern Adriatic seabed. The transition from a planktonic to a benthic lifestyle occurs when the developing larva attains a shell length at metamorphosis of just 0.1 cm , a diminutive size that underscores the vulnerability of the pediveliger stage during settlement onto suitable hard substrata like coralline algae or submerged rock faces. Field surveys of sub-littoral populations indicate that the shell length at puberty is approximately 1 cm [Lp = approximately 1 cm], a threshold at which gametogenic activity is first observed histologically in the gonadal tissues of the bivalve. This size at the onset of reproductive maturity represents about one-seventh of the species' maximal linear dimension, a proportion that aligns broadly with the maturation schedule reported for other slow-growing arcid bivalves inhabiting similar thermal regimes.

The reproductive physiology of Arca noae has been investigated through controlled laboratory experiments designed to estimate the species' maximum reproductive rate. At a stable water temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C], gravid females held individually in flow-through chambers and fed ad libitum on a mixed phytoplankton diet were recorded as producing approximately 13,700 fertilizable oocytes per day [Ri = approximately 13,700 fertilizable oocytes per day], a value derived from extrapolating the daily spawning output of individuals with an assumed shell length of 3 centimeters. This level of gamete release is comparatively modest for a bivalve of this size, likely reflecting the energetic constraints imposed by the species' relatively low tissue turnover and its investment in a robust, thick shell. The daily spawning rate, measured under stable thermal conditions, provides a useful benchmark for gauging the species' reproductive potential in its native Mediterranean habitat, where summer water temperatures frequently approach or exceed this experimental temperature regime.

Biometric analyses of dried soft tissues from a size-stratified sample of adult Noah's ark shells reveal that the ultimate dry weight approaches 2.3 g  in the largest specimens, a measurement that corresponds to a total shell length of approximately 7 centimeters. This dry mass, representing the ash-free organic component following removal of the calcified valves, is accumulated over a protracted growth period that spans multiple years. In striking contrast, the wet weight at birth is an astonishingly low 0.000000058 grams [Wwb = 0.000000058 grams], reflecting the minute diameter of the spawned oocytes, which average approximately 55 micrometers in diameter. The tremendous disparity between the birth mass and the ultimate adult dry mass—spanning roughly eight orders of magnitude—highlights the prodigious growth trajectory that the species must sustain throughout its early post-settlement life, when somatic tissue accretion is most rapid before the onset of reproductive maturation.

The oldest documented individuals of Arca noae collected from natural populations in the northern Adriatic Sea exhibit a lifespan of approximately 5,840 days [am = approximately 5,840 days], a longevity estimate that was derived from internal shell growth increment counts validated by mark-recapture studies conducted at a mean annual water temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C]. This maximum recorded lifespan of about 16 years places the Noah's ark shell among the longer-lived bivalves of the Mediterranean infauna, a pattern consistent with its robust shell morphology and relatively low metabolic rate. The sustained survival over nearly six decades (in days) is thought to be facilitated by the species' ability to withdraw into a tightly sealed shell cavity, a defense mechanism that offers considerable protection against both predators and physical disturbance. Such extended longevity has direct implications for population dynamics, as older individuals can contribute to reproductive output across many breeding seasons.

Comparative studies of arcid bivalves indicate that the shell length at puberty of 1 cm [Lp = 1 cm] in Arca noae is reached relatively early in the species' life, given that it entails only about a tenfold increase from the metamorphic size of 0.1 cm . This early maturation, achieved while the animal still retains considerable growth potential toward the ultimate shell height of 3.5 cm [Li = 3.5 cm], allows individuals to begin gamete production well before attaining maximal body dimensions, thereby spreading reproductive effort across a protracted adult lifespan. The reproductive strategy is further characterized by a sustained daily output of approximately 13,700 fertilizable oocytes [Ri = daily output of approximately 13,700 fertilizable oocytes] at the experimental temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C], which together with the extreme fecundity implied by the minute mass at birth of 0.000000058 grams [Wwb = 0.000000058 grams], suggests a classic r-selected element embedded within an otherwise K-selected, long-lived life history. The ultimate dry weight of 2.3 g  represents the culmination of this somatic investment, achieved over a lifespan of approximately 5,840 days [am = approximately 5,840 days] at a temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C].
